newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-London Exchange tightens AIM listing rules.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-London Exchange tightens AIM listing rules.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange (LSE) on Monday further tightened its rules for companies joining its Alternative Investment Market (AIM), saying it aimed to ensure greater disclosure of companies' activities and trading progress.
The updated rules, in a 15 page document sent to all AIM participants, follow the fourth review of AIM rules since its inception in June 1995.
The LSE said the latest rule changes were a fine-tuning exercise designed to make sure all the AIM market's participants adhere to the best practices of the majority.
"We are really underlining in black and white normal market practices which most people observe," said an LSE spokesman.
AIM was created to allow companies a quicker and less stringent method of raising equity. It has over 270 companies listed, with a total market capitalisation of nearly six billion stg.

Yet the LSE has had to balance its objective of creating a healthy dynamic market with the need to ensure that financial advisers keep to the rules and that unsuitable firms are not promoted to a listing.
The new proposals involve the requirement of companies to disclose the name of anyone who has received fees or shares worth 10,000 stg or more in the 12 months prior to joining AIM.
"This will ensure the disclosure of anyone who is in an influential position in or connected to the company," said a spokesman at the LSE.
In a similar vein, details of any company shadow directors - individuals who perform the role of a director without being appointed as such - will have to be given.
Another proposal is that companies should inform the market immediately if they believe their public profits forecasts in admission documents look inaccurate.

So far few companies have lost their AIM listing though one example was Firecrest Group Plc FIR.L, whose nomad resigned in August last year, resulting in Firecrest's shares being expelled from AIM when it failed to find a replacement.
The LSE is attempting to keep such embarrassing incidents to a minimum by placing greater emphasis on nomads satisfying themselves that companies are appropriate for admission to AIM.

The final version of the rules will be published at the end of June. Participants include LSE member firms, public relations companies and merchant banks who have until June 16 to return their comments.
